name: Compound interest
title: What Is Compound Interest? Definition and Example
description: Compound interest earns interest on earlier interest. See a three-year example, the formula, and how compounding differs from simple interest.
definition: Compound interest is interest calculated on both the original principal and interest already added to the balance.
explanation: When earnings stay invested, they become part of the amount earning the next period’s return. At a fixed positive rate, the interest earned each period grows even when you add no new money. The compounding frequency tells you how often interest is added; monthly and annual nominal rates need equivalent-rate conversion before comparison.
formula: Future value = principal × (1 + annual nominal rate / periods per year)^(periods per year × years)
formulaNote: Use rates as decimals: 4% is 0.04. This formula assumes a constant rate, no extra deposits or withdrawals, and no taxes or fees.

example.title: $1,500 growing at 4% for three years
example.intro: Start with $1,500 and compound once each year at a hypothetical 4% annual rate.
example.answer: Total interest is $187.30, versus $180 with simple interest on the original $1,500.
example.assumptions: Annual compounding; no contributions, withdrawals, taxes or fees. Carry full precision until the displayed result.

pitfall.title: Compounding is a mechanism, not a promised return
pitfall.text: A savings rate may change and investment returns can be negative. A smooth fixed-rate projection does not represent market volatility. Simple interest, by comparison, is calculated on the original principal without earning interest on prior interest.

name: CAGR
title: What Is CAGR? Compound Annual Growth Rate Explained
description: CAGR expresses growth between two values as one annual compounded rate. Learn the formula, see an example, and understand its cash-flow limitations.
definition: CAGR, or compound annual growth rate, is the constant yearly growth rate that would turn a beginning value into an ending value over a specified number of years.
explanation: It summarizes the endpoints as an annual compounded rate. CAGR can describe an investment balance, revenue or sales, but its interpretation depends on what the values represent. For investment performance, the simple endpoint formula assumes no intervening external deposits or withdrawals. Reinvested income must already be included in the ending value to measure total return.
formula: CAGR = (ending value / beginning value)^(1 / years) − 1
formulaNote: Multiply the decimal result by 100 for a percentage. Use a positive beginning value, a nonnegative ending value and a positive elapsed period.

example.title: $8,000 becoming $10,648 in three years
example.intro: Suppose an investment grows from $8,000 to $10,648 with no external cash flows.
example.answer: CAGR is 10% per year. Dividing 33.1% by three gives about 11.03%, which does not reproduce the ending value when compounded.
example.assumptions: Three full years; no external deposits or withdrawals. Values and any reinvested income are measured consistently.

pitfall.title: CAGR hides the path between the endpoints
pitfall.text: A 10% CAGR does not mean the investment gained 10% every year. Very different gains and losses can produce the same endpoints. New contributions can also increase an account balance without representing investment growth; use a cash-flow-aware method such as IRR when appropriate.

name: Real rate of return
title: What Is Real Rate of Return? Inflation-Adjusted Example
description: Real return measures the change in purchasing power after inflation. See the exact formula and why subtracting inflation is only an approximation.
definition: Real rate of return measures how much an investment’s purchasing power changes after adjusting its nominal return for inflation over the same period.
explanation: Nominal return describes the change in money value. Real return asks how much more or less that money can buy. A positive nominal return can still mean a loss of purchasing power when prices rise faster. An expected real return uses assumed inflation; a realized real return uses inflation measured over the investment period.
formula: Real return = (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation rate) − 1
formulaNote: Use decimal rates covering the same period. Subtracting inflation from nominal return is a convenient approximation, not the exact calculation.

example.title: An 8% return with 3% inflation
example.intro: An investment of $1,000 earns a hypothetical 8% over one year, while the price level rises 3%.
example.answer: Purchasing power rises about 4.85%, rather than the 5% given by simple subtraction.
example.assumptions: One year; the return and inflation rate cover the same dates. This example excludes taxes and fees.

pitfall.title: After inflation does not automatically mean after tax
pitfall.text: State whether the nominal return includes fees and taxes before comparing real returns. A broad price index also measures an average basket, so your own spending costs may change differently. Future inflation and returns are assumptions, not known outcomes.

name: Expense ratio
title: What Is an Expense Ratio? Fund Fees Explained
description: An expense ratio expresses a fund’s annual operating costs as a percentage of average net assets. See a cost example and avoid counting fees twice.
definition: An expense ratio is a fund’s annual operating expenses expressed as a percentage of its average net assets.
explanation: Mutual funds and ETFs pay operating expenses from fund assets, which reduces the return available to investors. The ratio is annual, even when expenses accrue throughout the year. It is not a fee charged on each purchase, and it does not include every possible cost of investing, such as all trading costs or a separately billed adviser fee. Check the prospectus for the applicable figure and any fee-waiver terms.
formula: Approximate annual cost = average invested balance × expense ratio
formulaNote: Use a decimal ratio: 0.25% is 0.0025. The dollar estimate assumes a constant average balance; actual accrual follows the fund’s practices.

example.title: A 0.25% expense ratio on $20,000
example.intro: Keep the balance at $20,000 for one year to isolate the fee arithmetic.
steps: With no return or new deposits, the simplified annual model ends at $19,950.
example.answer: The illustration costs $50 for the year. A 0.25% annual expense ratio is not a 25% charge.
example.assumptions: Zero gross return and no contributions or adviser fees. The calculator uses a simplified annual deduction, not the fund’s daily expense accrual.

pitfall.title: Check whether your return already includes the fee
pitfall.text: A fund’s published performance commonly already reflects operating expenses. Deducting the expense ratio again would count the same cost twice. The fee calculator’s After fund fees setting skips that second deduction; separately modeled adviser fees can still apply. Lower fees alone do not establish which investment is suitable.

name: Dollar-cost averaging
title: What Is Dollar-Cost Averaging? Example and Limitations
description: Dollar-cost averaging invests a fixed amount on a regular schedule. See how share purchases change with price and why the strategy can still lose money.
definition: Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same amount of money at regular intervals regardless of the current market price.
explanation: A fixed contribution buys more shares when prices are lower and fewer when they are higher. This makes the investment schedule consistent without requiring a price forecast. Investing new income as it arrives and gradually investing cash already available have different opportunity costs: money waiting in cash misses both gains and losses in the investment.
formula: Average purchase cost per share = total money invested / total shares purchased
formulaNote: For each purchase, shares = contribution / share price. The average cost is weighted by the number of shares bought, not a simple average of the purchase prices.

example.title: $120 invested on each of three dates
example.intro: Assume fractional shares are available and buy the same investment each time.
steps: First purchase at $12 per share: $120 / $12 = 10 shares.
Second purchase at $10 per share: $120 / $10 = 12 shares.
Third purchase at $8 per share: $120 / $8 = 15 shares.
example.answer: You invest $360 and own 37 shares, at an average cost of about $9.73 each. At the final $8 price, those shares are worth $296: a $64 loss.
example.assumptions: Three purchases; fractional shares allowed; no fees or dividends. Prices are hypothetical and are not a forecast.

pitfall.title: Buying more shares at lower prices does not guarantee a profit
pitfall.text: Losses remain possible, as the example shows. Phasing in a lump sum can also trail investing it immediately when prices rise. Our Investment Calculator estimates regular-contribution growth at an assumed constant return; it does not replay share prices or calculate the share-weighted cost shown above.

name: 401(k)
title: What Is a 401(k)? Contributions and Employer Match
description: A 401(k) is a U.S. employer-sponsored retirement plan. Learn the basics of contributions, traditional versus Roth treatment, matching and vesting.
definition: A 401(k) is a U.S. employer-sponsored retirement plan that lets eligible employees contribute part of their pay to a tax-advantaged retirement account.
explanation: Traditional pre-tax employee contributions generally defer federal income tax until withdrawal. A plan may also offer designated Roth contributions, made with after-tax pay; qualified Roth withdrawals are generally tax-free. Employers may add matching contributions under the plan’s formula. Your own elective deferrals are fully vested, while some employer contributions become yours over a vesting schedule.
formula: Illustrative employer match = salary × min(employee contribution rate, matched salary percentage) × match rate
formulaNote: This describes a simple single-tier match before legal and plan limits. Actual plans may use different tiers, eligibility, payroll timing and vesting rules.

example.title: A 50% match on the first 6% of salary
example.intro: Suppose the plan matches half of your contributions up to 6% of an eligible $50,000 annual salary, and you contribute 6%.
steps: Together, the deposits total $4,500 before any investment return.
example.answer: The 50% match adds $1,500. It does not mean the employer contributes 50% of your salary.
example.assumptions: A one-year arithmetic illustration using projection ages 30–31, a zero opening balance and zero return. It assumes eligibility, full vesting and no applicable cap reduction; the projection is before tax and fees.

pitfall.title: The account’s tax treatment is not its investment return
pitfall.text: Investment performance depends on the assets selected. Contribution limits change by year, and early withdrawals may face taxes and additional charges. Check the current IRS guidance and your plan document. Our projection states its modeled limit year and assumes full vesting; it does not determine your personal eligibility or traditional-versus-Roth tax outcome.

name: Amortization
title: What Is Loan Amortization? Principal and Interest Explained
description: Loan amortization pays down principal through scheduled payments. See how a payment splits into interest and principal, and what an amortization table shows.
definition: Loan amortization is the repayment of a loan’s principal through scheduled payments over time, with interest calculated under the loan’s terms.
explanation: For a fully amortizing fixed-rate loan with equal payments, each payment first covers the period’s interest and the remainder reduces principal. As the outstanding balance falls, the interest portion generally falls and the principal portion rises. An amortization schedule shows that split and the remaining balance after each payment. Here the term refers to loans, rather than the accounting treatment of intangible assets.
formula: Period interest = opening balance × period rate; principal repaid = payment − interest
formulaNote: A fully amortizing payment is chosen to clear the balance over the term. At a zero rate, the payment is simply principal divided by the number of payments.

example.title: The first payment on a $12,000, two-year loan
example.intro: Borrow $12,000 at a 6% nominal annual rate with 24 equal monthly payments.
steps: The level monthly payment is approximately $531.85.
First month’s interest: $12,000 × 0.5% = $60; about $471.85 goes to principal.
example.answer: The balance after the first payment is about $11,528.15. Later payments have a smaller interest portion as the balance declines.
example.assumptions: Monthly end-of-period payments; no fees, insurance, extra payments or rate changes. The calculator carries full precision, so lender schedules using payment-by-payment cent rounding can differ slightly.

pitfall.title: A fixed payment does not mean a fixed principal repayment
pitfall.text: The principal-and-interest split changes over the schedule. Mortgage taxes and insurance are separate from that split. A payment below the interest due may increase the balance, called negative amortization; an interest-only loan does not reduce principal during its interest-only period.

name: Markup vs. margin
title: Markup vs. Margin: Difference, Formulas and Example
description: Markup divides gross profit by cost; margin divides it by selling price. Compare both with a clear example and convert between the two percentages.
definition: Markup expresses gross profit as a percentage of cost, while gross profit margin expresses the same profit as a percentage of selling price.
explanation: Both start with selling price minus cost, but their denominators answer different questions. Markup describes the amount added to cost to set a price. Margin describes how much of each sales dollar remains after that cost. For a product calculation, specify what the cost includes and keep sales tax treatment consistent. Gross profit is not net profit after all business expenses.
formula: Markup = (price − cost) / cost; margin = (price − cost) / price
formulaNote: Multiply decimal ratios by 100 for percentages. With positive cost and price: margin = markup / (1 + markup), and markup = margin / (1 − margin).

example.title: A product costing $80 and selling for $100
example.intro: Use a cost of $80 and a selling price of $100, both excluding sales tax.
example.answer: The same $20 profit is a 25% markup and a 20% margin. A 25% margin would instead require a price of $80 / 0.75 ≈ $106.67.
example.assumptions: Positive unit cost and selling price; no sales tax. This compares product-level gross profit before other operating expenses.

pitfall.title: Do not enter a target margin as a markup
pitfall.text: Adding 20% to cost produces a 16.67% margin, not 20%. At positive cost, a 100% gross margin is unattainable at a finite price. A product’s positive gross margin also does not show whether sales cover rent, staff and other operating costs.

name: Simple interest
title: Simple interest: Definition, Formula and Example
description: Simple interest is interest calculated on principal without adding prior interest to the interest-bearing amount.
definition: Simple interest is interest calculated on principal without adding prior interest to the interest-bearing amount.
explanation: For an unchanged principal and rate, interest grows in proportion to elapsed time. If loan principal changes after payments, simple interest may instead accrue daily on the remaining principal. A one-deposit illustration is not a full repayment schedule.
formula: Interest = principal × annual rate × years; ending amount = principal + interest
formulaNote: Use a decimal rate and matching time units. Daily loan calculations also need the contract’s day-count convention.

name: APY
title: APY: Definition, Formula and Example
description: APY is a deposit’s annual percentage yield, expressing one year of interest growth with compounding under stated assumptions.
definition: APY is a deposit’s annual percentage yield, expressing one year of interest growth with compounding under stated assumptions.
explanation: A nominal rate alone does not specify the effect of compounding. Reinvesting interest more frequently raises the effective annual yield at the same positive nominal rate. U.S. disclosed APY follows Truth in Savings conventions, including timing assumptions; it is not an after-tax or inflation-adjusted return.
formula: Effective annual yield = (1 + nominal annual rate / compounding periods per year)^periods per year − 1
formulaNote: This regular-period formula assumes a constant rate and reinvested interest. Actual disclosures may use exact days; fees and withdrawals can change what you earn.

name: Inflation
title: Inflation: Definition, Formula and Example
description: Inflation is an increase in the general price level over a period, reducing how much a unit of money can buy.
definition: Inflation is an increase in the general price level over a period, reducing how much a unit of money can buy.
explanation: A consumer price index tracks a specified basket and population, rather than every household’s exact costs. A falling inflation rate still means prices are rising if the rate remains positive; a falling price level is deflation. Forecast inflation and observed index changes are different inputs.
formula: Inflation = ending price index / starting price index − 1; future equivalent cost = current cost × (1 + annual inflation)^years
formulaNote: Compare the same index and compatible periods. A constant annual rate is a projection, not a forecast of particular goods.

example.title: $1,000 of spending after two years at 3% inflation

pitfall.title: A higher account balance may still buy less
pitfall.text: Nominal growth can be smaller than inflation. Use the exact real-return relationship to compare purchasing power. Your rent, healthcare or education costs may also change differently from a broad index.

name: Time value of money
title: Time value of money: Definition, Formula and Example
description: The time value of money compares cash at different dates by accumulating or discounting it at a specified rate.
definition: The time value of money compares cash at different dates by accumulating or discounting it at a specified rate.
explanation: Present value translates future money into an equivalent amount at an earlier date. Future value compounds a current amount forward. The chosen rate reflects the comparison you are making; inflation, investment return and a risk-adjusted discount rate are not automatically interchangeable.
formula: Future value = present value × (1 + rate)^periods; present value = future value / (1 + rate)^periods
formulaNote: Rates and periods must match. These are lump-sum formulas; separate deposits and withdrawals require separate timing.

pitfall.text: A higher chosen discount rate reduces present value. That arithmetic does not establish the correct rate or guarantee payment. Compare cash flows in the same currency and use nominal cash flows with a nominal rate, or real cash flows with a real rate.

name: Return on investment (ROI)
title: Return on investment (ROI): Definition, Formula and Example
description: ROI expresses an investment’s gain or loss relative to its cost over a stated holding period.
definition: ROI expresses an investment’s gain or loss relative to its cost over a stated holding period.
explanation: Define proceeds, income and costs consistently. A total ROI does not adjust for how long the investment was held. Annualizing a single initial outlay and final receipt is different from measuring a portfolio with intervening deposits or withdrawals. For advertising, eCPM summarizes cost or revenue per 1,000 ad impressions. It does not include all the costs and receipts needed to establish ROI.
formula: ROI = (total amount received − investment cost) / investment cost
formulaNote: A positive cost is required. Include relevant income and fees consistently; multiply the ratio by 100 to show a percentage.

example.title: $2,500 returned from a $2,000 investment
example.intro: Assume all receipts arrive at the end of a two-year holding period.
example.answer: Total ROI is 25% over two years, not 25% per year.

pitfall.title: ROI does not measure risk or cash-flow timing
pitfall.text: Equal total ROI can come from different holding periods and different risks. Money added during the period must not be mistaken for investment profit. Use a cash-flow-aware method when dates and contributions matter.

name: Internal rate of return (IRR)
title: Internal rate of return (IRR): Definition, Formula and Example
description: IRR is a discount rate that makes the net present value of a specified series of cash flows equal to zero.
definition: IRR is a discount rate that makes the net present value of a specified series of cash flows equal to zero.
explanation: IRR incorporates the size and timing of contributions and distributions. Periodic IRR assumes equally spaced cash flows; a dated calculation needs an explicit day-count convention. The root may be absent or nonunique when cash flows change sign more than once.
formula: 0 = Σ[cash flow at period t / (1 + IRR)^t], including the initial cash flow at t = 0
formulaNote: Use signed cash flows from one consistent viewpoint. A periodic IRR is a rate per cash-flow period unless explicitly annualized.

example.title: $1,000 invested and $1,100 received a year later
example.intro: Treat the investment as an outflow and the receipt as an inflow.
example.answer: The annual IRR is 10% for these two cash flows.
example.assumptions: Exactly one year; no intermediate payments or extra fees.

pitfall.title: A higher IRR is not always the better project

name: Net present value (NPV)
title: Net present value (NPV): Definition, Formula and Example
description: NPV is the sum of cash inflows and outflows discounted to one valuation date using a stated discount rate.
definition: NPV is the sum of cash inflows and outflows discounted to one valuation date using a stated discount rate.
explanation: A positive NPV means the modeled cash flows exceed the return represented by the discount rate. It depends on the amounts, timing and chosen rate; it is not a guaranteed profit. Include the initial outlay and any terminal value once, with consistent signs.
formula: NPV = Σ[cash flow at period t / (1 + discount rate)^t]
formulaNote: Use a rate per cash-flow period and consistent nominal or real amounts. The t = 0 cash flow is not discounted.

name: Payback period
title: Payback period: Definition, Formula and Example
description: The payback period is the time needed for cumulative net cash inflows to recover an initial investment.
definition: The payback period is the time needed for cumulative net cash inflows to recover an initial investment.
explanation: Simple payback uses undiscounted cash flows. Discounted payback first discounts each receipt and therefore usually takes longer at a positive discount rate. Neither measure, by itself, evaluates cash flows after recovery.

name: Bond yield
title: Bond yield: Definition, Formula and Example
description: Bond yield relates a bond’s income or promised cash flows to its price; current yield and yield to maturity measure different things.
definition: Bond yield relates a bond’s income or promised cash flows to its price; current yield and yield to maturity measure different things.
explanation: The coupon rate uses face value as its denominator. Current yield divides the annual coupon by today’s price. Yield to maturity is the discount rate matching the price to the scheduled coupons and principal repayment, assuming those payments occur.

name: Certificate of deposit (CD)
title: Certificate of deposit (CD): Definition, Formula and Example
description: A certificate of deposit is a time deposit that generally holds money for a specified term under stated interest and withdrawal conditions.
definition: A certificate of deposit is a time deposit that generally holds money for a specified term under stated interest and withdrawal conditions.
explanation: Traditional bank CDs often offer a fixed rate, while other structures may have variable or callable features. Withdrawing early can reduce earnings or principal through a penalty. A brokered CD sold before maturity may receive a market price rather than its original deposit amount.
formula: For a fixed rate with reinvested interest: maturity value = principal × (1 + rate per period)^periods
formulaNote: Check APY, interest-crediting frequency, maturity, renewal terms and withdrawal rules. Deposit-insurance eligibility and limits depend on the institution and ownership category.

name: Arithmetic vs. geometric return
title: Arithmetic vs. geometric return: Definition, Formula and Example
description: Arithmetic average return is the simple mean of periodic returns; geometric average return is the constant compounded rate matching their cumulative growth.
definition: Arithmetic average return is the simple mean of periodic returns; geometric average return is the constant compounded rate matching their cumulative growth.
explanation: An arithmetic mean describes an average single-period outcome. The geometric mean describes linked growth over the full sequence, before external cash-flow effects. Volatility can leave the arithmetic mean positive while compounded wealth is unchanged or lower.
formula: Arithmetic mean = Σ returns / number of periods; geometric mean = [Π(1 + return)]^(1 / number of periods) − 1
formulaNote: Use equally long periods. Standard investment growth factors must be nonnegative; a −100% period wipes out the invested amount.

name: Annuity

description: In finance mathematics, an annuity is a series of equally spaced payments; an insurance annuity is a contract that may provide income under specified terms.
definition: In finance mathematics, an annuity is a series of equally spaced payments; an insurance annuity is a contract that may provide income under specified terms.
explanation: An ordinary annuity pays at period end; an annuity due pays at period beginning. A mathematical payment stream can last for a fixed term. Lifetime insurance income also depends on mortality assumptions, contract options, charges and the insurer’s ability to pay.

name: Loan-to-value ratio (LTV)
title: Loan-to-value ratio (LTV): Definition, Formula and Example
description: LTV compares a loan balance with a stated property value; combined LTV includes the relevant loans secured by the same property.
definition: LTV compares a loan balance with a stated property value; combined LTV includes the relevant loans secured by the same property.

name: Refinance break-even
title: Refinance break-even: Definition, Formula and Example
description: A simple refinance break-even is the time for assumed payment savings to recover refinancing costs; a full economic comparison also considers balances and cash-flow timing.
definition: A simple refinance break-even is the time for assumed payment savings to recover refinancing costs; a full economic comparison also considers balances and cash-flow timing.
explanation: The old and new loans may have different remaining terms, principal amounts and fee treatment. Lowering the payment by restarting a long term can increase lifetime interest. Cash-out proceeds are new borrowing rather than free savings.

name: Cap rate vs. cash-on-cash return
title: Cap Rate vs. Cash-on-Cash Return: Formulas and Financing Examples
description: Compare cap rate and cash-on-cash return on the same property. Five scenarios separate NOI, loan payments, closing costs and capital reserves.
definition: Cap rate compares property net operating income with a stated property value; cash-on-cash return compares pretax cash flow after debt service with cash invested.
explanation: Net operating income generally deducts operating expenses and vacancy but excludes financing, depreciation and income tax. Cash-on-cash depends on borrowing terms and the definition of invested cash. Closing costs, initial repairs and reserves must be included consistently when relevant.

formulaNote: State whether property value means purchase price, current value or total acquisition cost. Neither ratio alone includes every appreciation, sale or tax effect.

scope: Annual USD property comparison. Cap rate uses before-capex NOI and the entered price or value; cash-on-cash uses cash flow after financing and any stated capital reserve. No appreciation, sale, owner income tax or total return is implied.

comparison.heading: Same property, five financing and reserve scenarios
paragraphs: Hold the purchase price at $300,000 and annual NOI at $18,000. Every case has a 6% cap rate. Include $5,000 cash-paid closing costs, no repairs or initial reserve cash, and a 30-year amortizing loan where financed. Rent is $2,500 per month, vacancy and other income are zero, and operating expenses are $1,000 per month.

At 80% LTV and 5% loan interest, first-year P&I is $15,460.46. Annual cash flow is $2,539.54 on $65,000 cash invested, or 3.91%. At 8% interest it becomes −$3,132.42, or −4.82%, although the cap rate remains 6%. Adding a $100 monthly capital reserve lowers cash yield further to −6.67%.

Even the cash purchase has a 5.90% cash yield because its $305,000 cash basis includes closing costs while cap rate divides NOI by the $300,000 property price. Neither result is wrong; their denominators answer different questions. A higher cap rate is not automatically a better investment, and cash-on-cash is not IRR.

questions.question: Is cap rate the same as cash-on-cash return?
questions.answer: No. Cap rate relates before-financing NOI to property value; cash-on-cash relates the stated cash flow to cash invested. They can differ without borrowing when closing costs or reserves change the cash basis.

questions.question: Which should I use for a financed rental?
questions.answer: Use both for different purposes: operating yield before financing, and the cash yield of your funding arrangement. Also review downside, reserves and eventual sale; neither percentage measures all risks or total return.

name: Marginal vs. effective tax rate
title: Marginal vs. effective tax rate: Definition, Formula and Example
description: A marginal tax rate applies to an additional amount of taxable income; an effective tax rate divides a stated tax amount by a stated income measure.
definition: A marginal tax rate applies to an additional amount of taxable income; an effective tax rate divides a stated tax amount by a stated income measure.
explanation: In a progressive system, different layers of taxable income face different rates. Entering a higher bracket does not ordinarily apply that rate to all earlier layers. Credits, phaseouts and other taxes can affect the actual tax change from extra earnings.

name: Sales tax vs. VAT

name: Break-even point
title: Break-even point: Definition, Formula and Example
description: The break-even point is the sales volume or revenue at which total revenue equals the included fixed and variable costs.
definition: The break-even point is the sales volume or revenue at which total revenue equals the included fixed and variable costs.
explanation: Each unit’s contribution covers a share of fixed costs before profit begins. A single-product model assumes a constant selling price, variable cost per unit and fixed-cost total over the relevant activity range. Different product mixes need a consistent weighted contribution assumption.
formula: Break-even units = fixed costs / (unit price − unit variable cost); break-even revenue = fixed costs / contribution margin ratio
formulaNote: The unit contribution must be positive for a finite break-even with positive fixed costs. Round units up when only whole units can be sold.

name: Contribution margin

description: Contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs, showing the amount available to cover fixed costs and then profit.
definition: Contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs, showing the amount available to cover fixed costs and then profit.
explanation: Unlike gross profit, which uses the accounting cost-of-goods-sold classification, contribution margin separates costs by behavior. Some production overhead can be fixed, and some selling costs can be variable. Define the relevant sales volume and period before comparing ratios.
formula: Unit contribution = unit price − unit variable cost; contribution margin ratio = contribution / revenue
formulaNote: Revenue and variable costs must cover the same activity and period. Contribution is not net profit while fixed costs remain unpaid.

name: Depreciation

description: Depreciation allocates a tangible asset’s depreciable cost over its estimated useful life; it does not directly measure market value or set aside cash.
definition: Depreciation allocates a tangible asset’s depreciable cost over its estimated useful life; it does not directly measure market value or set aside cash.
explanation: Straight-line depreciation allocates equal amounts over full periods. Accelerated methods allocate more in earlier periods. Residual value, useful life, placed-in-service timing and accounting or tax conventions affect the schedule.

name: Percentage vs. percentage points
title: Percentage vs. percentage points: Definition, Formula and Example
description: Percentage points measure the arithmetic difference between percentage rates; percentage change measures the difference relative to a starting value.
definition: Percentage points measure the arithmetic difference between percentage rates; percentage change measures the difference relative to a starting value.
explanation: A move from 5% to 6% is one percentage point but a 20% relative increase in the rate. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. Always name the base when describing a percentage increase, discount, tip or margin. For example, an ad eCPM rising from $3 to $3.60 increases by 20%. This is a relative percentage change, not a percentage-point change: eCPM is a currency amount per 1,000 impressions, not a percentage rate.
formula: Relative change = (new value − old value) / old value × 100%; percentage-point change = new percentage − old percentage
formulaNote: Relative change is undefined when the old value is zero. Negative starting values require additional interpretation; a percentage-point difference does not require division.

name: Coast FIRE
title: What Is Coast FIRE? Meaning, Number & Example
description: Coast FIRE is a future-retirement savings milestone. Learn the meaning, inflation-adjusted formula and why reaching the number does not fund retirement today.
definition: Coast FIRE is a planning milestone where an invested retirement portfolio is projected to grow to a future retirement target without further contributions, assuming it is left invested and the chosen return and spending assumptions hold.
explanation: The Coast FIRE number discounts a future retirement portfolio target back to the current age. More time lowers the required starting amount when the assumed inflation-adjusted return is positive; less time raises it. Reaching the number concerns future retirement saving. You still need a separate way to pay living expenses during the coast period, and the result needs reassessment when investments or spending plans change.
formula: Coast number = (annual portfolio-funded spending / withdrawal rate) / (1 + real annual return)^years; real annual return = (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation) − 1
formulaNote: Use decimal rates and the years from current age to target retirement age. Budget, target and Coast number share today’s purchasing power. This is a constant-return present-value model; the withdrawal assumption sizes a target and does not prove its sustainability.

example.title: A future $1 million target needs a smaller portfolio today
example.intro: Consider a hypothetical person aged 35 targeting retirement at 65 with $40,000 annual portfolio-funded spending in today’s USD. Use a 4% withdrawal assumption, 7% nominal return after fees and 2.5% inflation.
steps: The future portfolio target is $40,000 / 0.04 = $1,000,000 in today’s purchasing power.
Exact real annual return is 1.07 / 1.025 − 1, approximately 4.39024%.
example.answer: The modeled Coast FIRE number today is $275,551.41. That is a savings milestone for age 65, not $1 million available at 35.
example.assumptions: All amounts in today’s USD; constant effective returns; no deposits or withdrawals in the no-contribution path; no automatic taxes, benefits or account-access rules. Defaults are illustrative.

pitfall.title: Reaching Coast FIRE is not the same as being able to retire now
pitfall.text: A Coast plan relies on leaving the portfolio invested until the target retirement age. Drawing from it earlier to cover living costs changes the plan. Barista FIRE commonly means supplementing work income with portfolio withdrawals, so it is not interchangeable with this no-withdrawal Coast model. Neither label establishes that a chosen withdrawal rate is safe.

scope: A planning concept, not a regulated account type, benefit entitlement or tax rule. FIRE abbreviates Financial Independence, Retire Early; a Coast plan may still target a conventional retirement age.

name: Net operating income (NOI)
title: What Is Net Operating Income? NOI Formula & Example
description: Net operating income is a property’s effective operating revenue minus property-level operating expenses, before financing, capital expenditure, depreciation and owner income tax.
definition: Net operating income is a property’s effective operating revenue minus property-level operating expenses, before financing, capital expenditure, depreciation and owner income tax.
explanation: Effective revenue accounts for the modeled rental vacancy loss and other operating income. Compare properties using the same period and expense definition. The result does not tell you how much cash remains after paying a mortgage or replacing major assets.
formula: NOI = scheduled rent − vacancy and collection loss + other operating income − operating expenses
formulaNote: Use one property or a consistently combined property portfolio and one reporting period. Dollar entries are monthly or annual as selected, in USD; changing that selector reinterprets rather than converts the values. Vacancy applies only to scheduled rent; other income must already reflect its own losses. Expenses are entered dollar amounts. NOI excludes debt service, owner income tax, depreciation, capital expenditure and replacement reserves. Lenders may use different reserve-adjusted definitions. Negative NOI is allowed; ratios are undefined at zero effective income.

example.title: Turn monthly rent and operating costs into annual NOI
example.intro: period: Monthly; rent: 4000; other_income: 100; vacancy: 5; taxes: 400; insurance: 150; repairs: 250; management: 300; utilities: 100; hoa: 0; other_expenses: 50.
steps: Scheduled rent $4,000 less 5% loss gives $3,800; add $100 other income for $3,900 monthly effective income.
Operating costs total $1,250 per month. NOI = $3,900 − $1,250 = $2,650.
example.answer: Annual NOI is $31,800; monthly equivalent $2,650 before financing and capital costs.
example.assumptions: Use one property or a consistently combined property portfolio and one reporting period. Dollar entries are monthly or annual as selected, in USD; changing that selector reinterprets rather than converts the values. Vacancy applies only to scheduled rent; other income must already reflect its own losses. Expenses are entered dollar amounts. NOI excludes debt service, owner income tax, depreciation, capital expenditure and replacement reserves. Lenders may use different reserve-adjusted definitions. Negative NOI is allowed; ratios are undefined at zero effective income.

pitfall.title: NOI is not cash after financing
pitfall.text: This model includes entered property taxes, insurance, routine repairs, management, owner-paid utilities, association charges and other operating costs. Expense classification matters: use the other-cost field only for operations, not a new roof, debt principal, interest or owner income tax. A lender may apply separate replacement reserves or underwriting adjustments.

name: FIRE number
title: What Is a FIRE Number? Formula and Spending Example
description: A FIRE number is a portfolio-sizing target obtained by dividing annual portfolio-funded retirement spending by an assumed withdrawal rate.
definition: A FIRE number is a portfolio-sizing target obtained by dividing annual portfolio-funded retirement spending by an assumed withdrawal rate.
explanation: FIRE abbreviates Financial Independence, Retire Early. A full target differs from a Coast milestone: Coast discounts a later target to a required balance now. Meeting a savings target does not establish whether the portfolio can support actual retirement withdrawals.
formula: FIRE number = annual portfolio-funded spending / assumed annual withdrawal rate
formulaNote: A single current age and projection age limit, with all money in today’s USD. Constant effective nominal return is adjusted for inflation using the exact real-growth relationship. Monthly investments maintain purchasing power and occur at month end. The path ends at the first full-target crossing or the age limit. No withdrawals after FIRE, random or historical returns, success probability, benefit eligibility, tax return, contribution cap or early-account-access rules are modeled. Four percent and the default return are illustrations, not assurances of safe retirement.

example.title: Reach a $1 million full FIRE target with monthly investing
example.intro: age: 35; max_age: 80; balance: 150000; spending: 40000; monthly: 2000; return: 7; inflation: 2.5; withdrawal: 4.
steps: Annual portfolio-funded spending $40,000 / 4% = $1,000,000 in today’s USD.
Exact real return = 1.07 / 1.025 − 1 = approximately 4.39024%. Start with $150,000 and add $2,000 at each month end.
The first whole-month crossing occurs after 221 months. Deposits and the savings projection stop there.
example.answer: The modeled target crossing is age 53 years, 5 months. Total new investments are $442,000 and the endpoint is $1,003,515.17 in today’s USD; this is not a withdrawal-sustainability result.
example.assumptions: A single current age and projection age limit, with all money in today’s USD. Constant effective nominal return is adjusted for inflation using the exact real-growth relationship. Monthly investments maintain purchasing power and occur at month end. The path ends at the first full-target crossing or the age limit. No withdrawals after FIRE, random or historical returns, success probability, benefit eligibility, tax return, contribution cap or early-account-access rules are modeled. Four percent and the default return are illustrations, not assurances of safe retirement.

pitfall.title: A sizing target is not a withdrawal guarantee
pitfall.text: It grows your invested assets with an exact inflation-adjusted monthly rate and adds the monthly investment at month end. It reports the first whole month meeting the full FIRE target, then ends the projection. If the selected age limit arrives first, it reports no crossing within that horizon rather than extrapolating an unsupported retirement age.

name: Modified internal rate of return (MIRR)
title: What Is MIRR? Modified Return Formula & Example
description: MIRR is an equivalent return for equally spaced project cash flows after separately discounting payments at a financing rate and compounding receipts at a reinvestment rate.
definition: MIRR is an equivalent return for equally spaced project cash flows after separately discounting payments at a financing rate and compounding receipts at a reinvestment rate.
explanation: Unlike IRR, MIRR uses two explicit rate assumptions to transform the signed cash flows. The period count is one fewer than the complete number of entries including time zero. Periodic and annualized rates differ for subannual cash-flow spacing.
formula: Periodic MIRR = (terminal value of positive flows / absolute present value of negative flows)^(1 / periods) − 1
formulaNote: Cash flows are USD amounts at equally spaced dates, with the first entry at time zero and 2–601 entries. At least one positive and one negative amount is required. Both financing and reinvestment inputs are effective annual rates; selected spacing converts them to equivalent period rates. Results show periodic and effective annual MIRR. Internal blank lines and labels are rejected instead of silently omitted; use explicit 0 for no-flow periods. No irregular-date XIRR, actual financing schedule, tax estimate, inflation adjustment or project accept/reject advice is supplied.

example.title: Reinvest annual project receipts at 10%
example.intro: flows: -10000, 3000, 4000, 5000; period: Annually; finance: 8; reinvest: 10.
steps: Time-zero outflow is $10,000. Receipts are $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 at the next three year ends.
example.answer: Annual MIRR is approximately 9.22318%. The financing rate does not change the time-zero-only payment.
example.assumptions: Cash flows are USD amounts at equally spaced dates, with the first entry at time zero and 2–601 entries. At least one positive and one negative amount is required. Both financing and reinvestment inputs are effective annual rates; selected spacing converts them to equivalent period rates. Results show periodic and effective annual MIRR. Internal blank lines and labels are rejected instead of silently omitted; use explicit 0 for no-flow periods. No irregular-date XIRR, actual financing schedule, tax estimate, inflation adjustment or project accept/reject advice is supplied.

pitfall.title: The ordering and rate convention matter
pitfall.text: IRR finds a discount rate that makes the net present value of the original cash-flow sequence zero; some sequences have multiple or no relevant IRRs. MIRR instead transforms outflows and inflows using separate entered rates, then reports an equivalent rate over the selected horizon. Its single output depends on those assumptions and is not proof that a project creates value.

tools.text: Modified internal rate of return separates the financing cost of project payments from the return assumed on reinvested receipts. The model discounts negative cash flows to time zero, compounds positive cash flows to the last period, then finds the equivalent growth rate between those two totals. Enter a complete signed series with equal spacing, including zero periods.

definition: Debt snowball is a repayment ordering method that directs extra funds to smaller balances while minimum payments continue on the rest.
explanation: Its focus is a sequence of cleared balances. A fixed payment budget can roll into the next target, but the interest cost still depends on the rates, timing and payment rules. An earlier milestone is not a promise about motivation.

name: Debt avalanche
title: Debt Avalanche: Meaning, Payment Order and Example
description: Debt avalanche prioritizes the highest interest rate after minimum payments, then redirects available extra money to the next rate.
definition: Debt avalanche is a repayment ordering method that directs extra funds to the highest APR while minimum payments continue on the rest.
explanation: Its focus is the rate applied to the outstanding balance rather than the debt’s size. A smaller debt can still clear through minimum payments first. Compare costs using a consistent budget and contractual assumptions.
formula: Available extra = total monthly debt budget − sum of capped minimum payments
formulaNote: The calculator uses descending APR, with entered order for equal rates. APR / 12 is a monthly approximation, not daily card interest.

example.title: Follow the first month of a $400 repayment budget
example.intro: Card A owes $5,000 at 22% APR with a $150 minimum; Card B owes $3,000 at 18% with a $100 minimum.
steps: Monthly interest is $91.6667 for A and $45 for B before display rounding.
After $250 in minimums, $150 remains for extra repayment.
Avalanche directs that extra to A; its month-one balance becomes about $4,791.67.
example.answer: With a fixed $400 budget, A clears in month 21 and both debts clear in month 25, with $1,823.78 modeled interest.
example.assumptions: Fixed rates and minimums; monthly interest before payments; no fees, new borrowing or one-time payment; full precision internally.

pitfall.title: A payment-order rule does not override loan terms
pitfall.text: Cover every required minimum and check actual interest, fees and due dates. A modeled payoff is not a settlement, account closure, credit-score prediction or instruction to miss a payment.

name: Barista FIRE
title: Barista FIRE: Meaning, Number and Income-Stop Example
description: Learn what Barista FIRE means, how a part-time income stop changes your number, and how it differs from Coast FIRE.
definition: Barista FIRE is an approach to leaving full-time work in which part-time earnings and portfolio withdrawals together pay living expenses before full retirement.
explanation: The job does not have to be in a coffee shop. The key distinction is the need for earned income alongside assets. A useful plan specifies when work begins, when the income ends, and the portfolio needed after work ends. There is no universal Barista FIRE dollar threshold.
formula: Required portfolio at transition = present value of monthly spending gaps + present value of full-retirement target
formulaNote: The full-retirement sizing target is later annual portfolio-funded spending divided by the withdrawal assumption. Monthly gaps are spending less after-tax earnings, floored at zero. The calculator values dated cash flows, not permanent part-time earnings.

example.title: A ten-year income bridge inside a twenty-year plan
example.intro: Start at age 45; income ends at 55; full retirement at 65. Bridge spending $36,000/year, after-tax income $24,000/year and later spending $24,000/year. Zero return and inflation, 4% terminal withdrawal assumption.
steps: From 45 to 55, the portfolio funds $12,000/year for 10 years: $120,000.
From 55 to 65, it funds the full $36,000/year for 10 years: $360,000.
The full-retirement target is $24,000 ÷ 0.04 = $600,000. At zero growth, add $120,000 + $360,000 + $600,000.
example.answer: The required transition portfolio is $1,080,000. Ignoring the earnings stop would understate the required bridge capital.
example.assumptions: Constant purchasing power; zero returns and inflation; month-end cash flows; no taxes or benefits calculated. A terminal target is not a safe-withdrawal guarantee.

pitfall.title: Do not assume part-time pay lasts forever
pitfall.text: Dividing the current spending gap by 4% can understate the need when earnings end before full retirement. Also check healthcare costs, access to retirement accounts, emergency reserves and variable investment returns.

name: Lean FIRE
title: Lean FIRE: Definition, Example and Limitations
description: Lean FIRE describes financial independence built around a lower-spending lifestyle; it has no universal income or wealth cutoff.
definition: Lean FIRE describes financial independence built around a lower-spending lifestyle; it has no universal income or wealth cutoff.
explanation: Start with the costs the portfolio must fund, including healthcare, recurring irregular expenses and an entered tax allowance. The calculator adds a buffer to the entire budget before sizing the full FIRE target. Avoid counting the same cost in more than one category. This is a full financial-independence target, unlike a discounted Coast FIRE threshold today.
formula: FIRE target = annual portfolio-funded budget / withdrawal assumption
formulaNote: Use the rate as a decimal. Default rates are illustrative; a target does not establish that later withdrawals are sustainable.

example.title: $30,000 annual spending at an illustrative 4% rate
example.intro: Assume today’s USD, no additional spending buffer and no separate benefits.
example.answer: The modeled full target is $750,000; the spending level does not define a universal Lean FIRE threshold.
example.assumptions: Target sizing only. No market path, withdrawal simulation, benefit timing or automatic tax calculation.

pitfall.title: A lifestyle label is not a safety test
pitfall.text: A smaller or larger budget changes the target, but does not determine market risk, account access or whether the spending plan is feasible. Review the withdrawal assumption and later spending separately.

name: Dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP)
title: Dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP): Definition, Example and Limitations
description: A dividend reinvestment plan uses dividend payments to buy additional shares rather than paying them out for the investor to retain as cash.
definition: A dividend reinvestment plan uses dividend payments to buy additional shares rather than paying them out for the investor to retain as cash.
explanation: Reinvestment changes the share count and exposure to the same investment. It is not an extra external contribution or a guarantee of higher wealth. Share-price changes and dividends per share are separate quantities; a total-return assumption already includes distributions and should not be entered as price appreciation plus another dividend yield.
formula: New shares from a payout = after-tax dividend cash / purchase price per share
formulaNote: Use actual plan prices, fees and fractional-share rules for a real account. The linked calculator uses hypothetical prices and fractional shares.

example.title: A $100 quarterly dividend buys one share at $100
example.intro: Hold 100 shares at $100 with a 4% starting annual dividend yield, quarterly payment and no current dividend tax.
steps: At an unchanged $100 price, $100 buys one additional fractional-or-whole share.
example.answer: The position has 101 shares after the first payout, before any external deposit.
example.assumptions: Constant share price and dividend dollars per share; zero current dividend tax and no transaction costs.

pitfall.title: Reinvestment does not automatically remove dividend tax
pitfall.text: In a taxable account, using dividends to buy stock generally does not remove reporting obligations. Check account treatment and retain purchase records. More shares can still mean less wealth if their value falls.

name: Roth conversion ladder
title: Roth conversion ladder: Definition, Example and Limitations
description: A Roth conversion ladder stages conversions into a Roth IRA in successive tax years and plans later use of conversion principal during an early-retirement bridge.
definition: A Roth conversion ladder stages conversions into a Roth IRA in successive tax years and plans later use of conversion principal during an early-retirement bridge.
explanation: A conversion moves existing retirement assets; it is different from a regular annual contribution. Planning must distinguish the amount converted, estimated tax, regular contribution basis, conversion-principal records and available market value. Our calculator models one owner’s all-pre-tax traditional IRA without prior conversion lots or initial Roth earnings.
formula: Illustrative conversion tax = actual fully taxable conversion × entered flat tax assumption
formulaNote: This is a cash-planning approximation, not a tax-bracket calculation. A conversion clock does not qualify all earnings for withdrawal.

example.title: $40,000 converted with an illustrative 20% tax assumption
example.intro: Assume a calendar-year taxpayer converts in 2027 and pays tax from outside cash.
steps: The 2027 conversion’s five-tax-year date is January 1, 2032; assess distribution conditions separately.
example.answer: Budget $8,000 tax cash separately; the converted $40,000 is not the same as after-tax cash available immediately.
example.assumptions: Fully taxable conversion, no withholding from IRA funds, no bracket or eligibility calculation.

pitfall.title: Five years of living expenses may omit later conversion taxes
pitfall.text: The model may still need outside cash for new conversion taxes after seasoned principal starts covering living costs. Check the whole selected bridge. The detailed guide shows why $240,000 is insufficient in one eight-year example.

name: Roth IRA five-year rules
title: Roth IRA five-year rules: Definition, Example and Limitations
description: Roth IRA rules use different five-tax-year periods for qualified distributions and for certain early distributions attributable to conversion amounts; the two clocks answer different questions.
definition: Roth IRA rules use different five-tax-year periods for qualified distributions and for certain early distributions attributable to conversion amounts; the two clocks answer different questions.
explanation: IRS Publication 590-B describes a separate period for each conversion and a distinct qualified-distribution test. Regular contribution basis, converted amounts and earnings are different sources. Actual distribution ordering and possible exceptions depend on records and circumstances, not simply a five-year anniversary.
formula: Calendar-year conversion in Y: five-tax-year date = January 1 of Y + 5
formulaNote: This date concerns the conversion period. Qualified earnings also require the applicable Roth holding period and a qualifying condition, commonly age 59½; it is not a general withdrawal permission.

example.title: Two conversions, two dates
example.intro: Consider calendar-year conversions in 2027 and 2028.
steps: Those dates alone do not establish that earnings are qualified.
example.answer: Track conversion years separately and keep the qualified-distribution test distinct.
example.assumptions: General calendar-year illustration; no exception or eligibility determination.

pitfall.title: Seasoned principal is not the entire Roth balance
pitfall.text: Investment growth does not create more conversion principal. Losses can also leave market value below principal records. Do not read a conversion clock date as proof that all account dollars can be distributed without tax or additional tax.

name: Covered call
title: Covered call: Definition, Example and Limitations
description: A covered call combines ownership of shares with a short call on an equivalent share quantity, receiving a premium while limiting upside and retaining substantial stock downside.
definition: A covered call combines ownership of shares with a short call on an equivalent share quantity, receiving a premium while limiting upside and retaining substantial stock downside.
explanation: For a standard new buy-write in the calculator, one short contract covers exactly 100 purchased shares. At expiry, the stock plus short-call economic value is capped by the strike. The premium offsets part of initial cost but is not pure profit. Before-expiry values and actual assignment timing require more than an expiry payoff diagram.
formula: Expiry profit/loss = shares × min(expiry stock price, strike) − net initial debit − exit costs
formulaNote: Net debit includes share purchase and opening fees less premium. Premium is per share; contract fees and position-wide fees use different units.

example.title: 100 shares at $50 and a $55 call sold for $2 per share
example.intro: Assume one standard contract and zero fees.
steps: Net debit is $4,800; fee-free break-even price is $48.
At or above $55 at expiry, maximum economic profit is $5,500 − $4,800 = $700.
example.answer: Upside is capped at $700, while a zero stock value loses $4,800.
example.assumptions: Expiry-only new buy-write, no dividend, tax, financing or early-close model.

pitfall.title: Covered does not mean protected against a stock crash
pitfall.text: Early assignment can occur and gains above strike are limited. The simple annualized maximum return is not APY or repeatable income. Adjusted contracts, uncovered calls and existing holdings’ tax basis require other analysis.
